    Euclidean-like Algorithm

    Introduction

    The Euclidean-like algorithm was proposed by Hong Huadun during the 2016 winter camp exchange. It is commonly used to solve summation problems of sequences in the form:

    ⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋⌊ai+bc⌋

    (indexed by 𝑖i). Its main idea is to use the recursive structure of fractions to transform the problem into smaller ones and solve recursively. Because there is a direct relationship between the recursive structure of fractions and the Euclidean algorithm, this summation method is also called the Euclidean-like algorithm.

    Since continued fractions and Stern-Brocot trees also describe the recursive structure of fractions, problems that can be solved using the Euclidean-like algorithm can usually be solved by these methods as well. Compared to these methods, the Euclidean-like algorithm is usually easier to understand, and its implementation is more straightforward.

    Euclidean-like Algorithm

    The simplest example is the summation problem:

    𝑓(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑖=0⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋,f(a,b,c,n)=∑i=0n⌊ai+bc⌋,

    where 𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛a,b,c,n are all positive integers.

    Algebraic Solution

    First, take 𝑎,𝑏a,b modulo 𝑐c to simplify the problem, transforming it to the case 0 ≤𝑎,𝑏 <𝑐0≤a,b<c:

    𝑓(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑖=0⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋=𝑛∑𝑖=0⌊(⌊𝑎𝑐⌋𝑐+(𝑎mod𝑐))𝑖+(⌊𝑏𝑐⌋𝑐+(𝑏mod𝑐))𝑐⌋=𝑛∑𝑖=0(⌊𝑎𝑐⌋𝑖+⌊𝑏𝑐⌋+⌊(𝑎mod𝑐)𝑖+(𝑏mod𝑐)𝑐⌋)=𝑛(𝑛+1)2⌊𝑎𝑐⌋+(𝑛+1)⌊𝑏𝑐⌋+𝑓(𝑎mod𝑐,𝑏mod𝑐,𝑐,𝑛).f(a,b,c,n)=∑i=0n⌊ai+bc⌋=∑i=0n⌊(⌊ac⌋c+(amodc))i+(⌊bc⌋c+(bmodc))c⌋=∑i=0n(⌊ac⌋i+⌊bc⌋+⌊(amodc)i+(bmodc)c⌋)=n(n+1)2⌊ac⌋+(n+1)⌊bc⌋+f(amodc,bmodc,c,n).

    Now consider the transformed problem. Let:

    𝑚=⌊𝑎𝑛+𝑏𝑐⌋.m=⌊an+bc⌋.

    Then the original problem can be written as a double summation:

    𝑛∑𝑖=0⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋=𝑛∑𝑖=0𝑚−1∑𝑗=0[𝑗<⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋].∑i=0n⌊ai+bc⌋=∑i=0n∑j=0m−1[j<⌊ai+bc⌋].

    Swap the order of summation, which requires finding the range of 𝑖i that satisfies the condition for each 𝑗j. For this, transform the condition:

    𝑗<⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋=⌈𝑎𝑖+𝑏+1𝑐⌉−1⟺𝑗+1<⌈𝑎𝑖+𝑏+1𝑐⌉⟺𝑗+1<𝑎𝑖+𝑏+1𝑐⟺𝑐𝑗+𝑐−𝑏−1𝑎<𝑖⟺⌊𝑐𝑗+𝑐−𝑏−1𝑎⌋<𝑖.j<⌊ai+bc⌋=⌈ai+b+1c⌉−1⟺j+1<⌈ai+b+1c⌉⟺j+1<ai+b+1c⟺cj+c−b−1a<i⟺⌊cj+c−b−1a⌋<i.

    The transformation process uses the properties of floor and ceiling functions. Substituting the transformed condition, the original formula can be written as:

    𝑓(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑚−1∑𝑗=0𝑛∑𝑖=0[𝑖>⌊𝑐𝑗+𝑐−𝑏−1𝑎⌋]=𝑚−1∑𝑗=0(𝑛−⌊𝑐𝑗+𝑐−𝑏−1𝑎⌋)=𝑛𝑚−𝑓(𝑐,𝑐−𝑏−1,𝑎,𝑚−1).f(a,b,c,n)=∑j=0m−1∑i=0n[i>⌊cj+c−b−1a⌋]=∑j=0m−1(n−⌊cj+c−b−1a⌋)=nm−f(c,c−b−1,a,m−1).

    Let (𝑎′,𝑏′,𝑐′,𝑛′) =(𝑐,𝑐 −𝑏 −1,𝑎,𝑚 −1)(a′,b′,c′,n′)=(c,c−b−1,a,m−1), which again falls into the case 𝑎′ >𝑐′a′>c′ discussed earlier.

    Combining these two transformations, we can find that in the process, (𝑎,𝑐)(a,c) continuously takes mod and exchanges positions until 𝑎 =0a=0. This is similar to performing Euclidean algorithm on (𝑎,𝑐)(a,c), which is how the Euclidean-like algorithm gets its name. Its time complexity is 𝑂(log⁡min{𝑎,𝑐})O(log⁡min{a,c}).

    During computation, the case 𝑚 =0m=0 might occur, which leads to inner recursion with 𝑛 = −1n=−1. This does not affect the final result. However, if we terminate the algorithm when 𝑚 =0m=0 occurs, the time complexity can be improved to 𝑂(log⁡min{𝑎,𝑐,𝑛})O(log⁡min{a,c,n}).

    Explanation of Complexity

    Using the similarity with the Euclidean algorithm, it is easy to explain that its time complexity is 𝑂(log⁡min{𝑎,𝑐})O(log⁡min{a,c}). Therefore, we only need to explain that if we terminate the algorithm when 𝑚 =0m=0, the time complexity is also 𝑂(log⁡𝑛)O(log⁡n).

    Let 𝑚 =⌊(𝑎𝑛 +𝑏)/𝑐⌋m=⌊(an+b)/c⌋, and denote 𝑆 =𝑚𝑛S=mn, 𝑘 =𝑚/𝑛k=m/n, which respectively correspond to the area and slope of the geometric diagram (see the next section). For sufficiently large 𝑛n, we have approximately 𝑘 ≐𝑎/𝑐k≐a/c.

    Observe the changes of 𝑆S and 𝑘k during the algorithm. In the first step of taking mod, 𝑛n remains unchanged, and 𝑘k changes from 𝑎/𝑐a/c to (𝑎mod𝑐)/𝑐(amodc)/c, which is equivalent to the slope changing from 𝑘k to 𝑘 −⌊𝑘⌋k−⌊k⌋, and 𝑆S also approximately becomes (𝑘 −⌊𝑘⌋)(k−⌊k⌋) times its original value. In the second step of swapping coordinates, 𝑆S remains approximately unchanged, while 𝑘k becomes its reciprocal. Therefore, if after the two steps the pair (𝑘,𝑆)(k,S) becomes (𝑘′,𝑆′)(k′,S′), we have 𝑘′ =(𝑘 −⌊𝑘⌋)−1k′=(k−⌊k⌋)−1 and 𝑆′ =(𝑘 −⌊𝑘⌋)𝑆S′=(k−⌊k⌋)S.

    Since 1 ≤⌊𝑘′⌋ ≤𝑘′ <⌊𝑘′⌋ +11≤⌊k′⌋≤k′<⌊k′⌋+1, after two rounds of recursive computation, the product reduction ratio is at least

    (𝑘′−⌊𝑘′⌋)(𝑘−⌊𝑘⌋)=1−⌊𝑘′⌋𝑘′<1−⌊𝑘′⌋⌊𝑘′⌋+1=1⌊𝑘′⌋+1≤12.(k′−⌊k′⌋)(k−⌊k⌋)=1−⌊k′⌋k′<1−⌊k′⌋⌊k′⌋+1=1⌊k′⌋+1≤12.

    Therefore, after at most 𝑂(log⁡𝑆)O(log⁡S) rounds, the algorithm must terminate. Because from the second round onwards, the 𝑆S at the beginning of each round is never more than the 𝑆S after the mod-taking of the previous round, and the latter is roughly 𝑘𝑛2kn2 with 𝑘 <1k<1, thus 𝑂(log⁡𝑆) ⊆𝑂(log⁡𝑛)O(log⁡S)⊆O(log⁡n). This gives the above conclusion.

    The reference implementation for the template problem is as follows:

    Template Problem Implementation (Library Checker - Sum of Floor of Linear)](https://judge.yosupo.jp/problem/sum_of_floor_of_linear)

    #include <iostream>

long long solve(long long a, long long b, long long c, long long n) {
  long long n2 = n * (n + 1) / 2;
  if (a >= c || b >= c)
    return solve(a % c, b % c, c, n) + (a / c) * n2 + (b / c) * (n + 1);
  long long m = (a * n + b) / c;
  if (!m) return 0;
  return m * n - solve(c, c - b - 1, a, m - 1);
}

int main() {
  int t;
  std::cin >> t;
  for (; t; --t) {
    int a, b, c, n;
    std::cin >> n >> c >> a >> b;
    std::cout << solve(a, b, c, n - 1) << '\n';
  }
  return 0;
}

    Geometric Interpretation

    This algorithm can also be understood geometrically. The problems that the Euclidean-like algorithm can solve are mainly integer point counting problems under a line.

    As shown in the leftmost part of the figure below, this summation is equivalent to counting the number of lattice points under the line

    𝑦=𝑎𝑥+𝑏𝑐y=ax+bc

    above the 𝑥x-axis (not including the 𝑥x-axis) and with 𝑥x-coordinate in [0,𝑛][0,n].

    First, remove the integer parts of the slope and intercept. This step corresponds to calculating the number of blue points in the middle part of the figure separately. When both the slope and intercept are integers, the blue points form a trapezoidal array, that is, the lattice points in different vertical columns form an arithmetic progression, so the number of these points is easy to calculate. After removing these points, the remaining lattice points are consistent with the red points in the rightmost part of the figure. The problem is transformed into the case where both the slope and intercept are less than one. Since the height of the trapezoid is 𝑛 +1n+1 and the lengths of the two bases are ⌊𝑏/𝑐⌋⌊b/c⌋ and (⌊𝑎/𝑐⌋𝑛 +⌊𝑏/𝑐⌋)(⌊a/c⌋n+⌊b/c⌋), using the formula for the area of a trapezoid, this step can be summarized as:

    𝑓(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑓(𝑎mod𝑐,𝑏mod𝑐,𝑐,𝑛)+12(𝑛+1)(⌊𝑏𝑐⌋+(⌊𝑎𝑐⌋𝑛+⌊𝑏𝑐⌋)).f(a,b,c,n)=f(amodc,bmodc,c,n)+12(n+1)(⌊bc⌋+(⌊ac⌋n+⌊bc⌋)).

    Then, flip the 𝑥x and 𝑦y axes. As shown in the leftmost part of the figure below, the red and blue points in the figure form a rectangular point array of horizontal length 𝑛n and vertical length 𝑚 =⌊(𝑎𝑛 +𝑏)/𝑐⌋m=⌊(an+b)/c⌋. To count the number of red points, we only need to count the number of blue points and subtract from the total of the rectangular point array. After flipping, the blue point array in the left part becomes the red point array under some line. Moreover, after flipping, the slope is greater than one, which again falls into the case already processed above.

    The key is how to compute the equation of the line above the new red point array. Flipping the 𝑥x and 𝑦y axes of the leftmost part gives the middle part. The line above the red point array after flipping (the solid line in the middle part) does not correspond to the line before flipping (the solid line in the leftmost part), but is the result of shifting the line before flipping slightly up and to the left (the dashed line in the leftmost part). This is because if we directly flip the line (the solid line in the leftmost part), we get the dashed line in the middle part, but by definition, the lattice points under it include those exactly on the line, which would lead to double counting of points on the line. To avoid this, after flipping the line, we shift the line 𝑦 =(𝑐𝑥 −𝑏)/𝑎y=(cx−b)/a downward slightly to get 𝑦 =(𝑐𝑥 −𝑏 −1)/𝑎y=(cx−b−1)/a, so that the point array under it is exactly the blue point array before flipping.

    There is another detail to handle. The intercept of the line in the middle part of the figure is negative, which means it has not yet returned to the initial case. To make the intercept non-negative, we only need to shift the line (the solid line in the middle part) left by one unit. This does not miss any lattice points because there are no points with zero 𝑦y-coordinate in the blue point array before flipping, and after flipping, there are no points with zero 𝑥x-coordinate. Finally, the line equation becomes 𝑦 =(𝑐𝑥 +𝑐 −𝑏 −1)/𝑎y=(cx+c−b−1)/a; at the same time, the upper bound of the 𝑥x-coordinate of the point array also changes from 𝑚m to 𝑚 −1m−1. This step can be summarized as:

    𝑓(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑚𝑛−𝑓(𝑐,𝑐−𝑏−1,𝑎,𝑚−1).f(a,b,c,n)=mn−f(c,c−b−1,a,m−1).

    This recursive algorithm works for two main reasons:

    • First, the slope of the line continuously takes its fractional part and then takes its reciprocal, which is equivalent to the continued fraction expansion of the line slope 𝑘 =𝑎/𝑐k=a/c. Since the length of the continued fraction expansion of a rational number is 𝑂(log⁡min{𝑎,𝑐})O(log⁡min{a,c}), this process must terminate after 𝑂(log⁡min{𝑎,𝑐})O(log⁡min{a,c}) steps;
    • Second, because when flipping the axes each time, the slope of the line is less than one, so intuitively we should have 𝑚 <𝑛m<n, that is, after such an iteration, the range of the 𝑥x-coordinate is always shrinking. The complexity calculation in the previous section strictly shows that after every two iterations, 𝑛n is at most half of the original, so this process must terminate after 𝑂(log⁡𝑛)O(log⁡n) steps.

    This is also the reason why the Euclidean-like algorithm has complexity 𝑂(log⁡min{𝑎,𝑐,𝑛})O(log⁡min{a,c,n}) when the slope is a rational number.

    Using a similar geometric interpretation, the Euclidean-like algorithm can be extended to the case where the slope is an irrational number. For a detailed analysis, see the example problems later.

    Example Problems

    Template Euclidean-like Algorithm

    Multiple queries. Given positive integers 𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛a,b,c,n, find:

    𝑓(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑖=0⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋,𝑔(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑖=0𝑖⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋,ℎ(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑖=0⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋2.f(a,b,c,n)=∑i=0n⌊ai+bc⌋,g(a,b,c,n)=∑i=0ni⌊ai+bc⌋,h(a,b,c,n)=∑i=0n⌊ai+bc⌋2.
    Solution One

    Similar to the derivation of 𝑓f, we can get the recursive expressions for 𝑔g and ℎh.

    First, using modulo to transform to 0 ≤𝑎,𝑏 <𝑐0≤a,b<c:

    𝑔(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑔(𝑎mod𝑐,𝑏mod𝑐,𝑐,𝑛)+⌊𝑎𝑐⌋𝑛(𝑛+1)(2𝑛+1)6+⌊𝑏𝑐⌋𝑛(𝑛+1)2,ℎ(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=ℎ(𝑎mod𝑐,𝑏mod𝑐,𝑐,𝑛)+2⌊𝑏𝑐⌋𝑓(𝑎mod𝑐,𝑏mod𝑐,𝑐,𝑛)+2⌊𝑎𝑐⌋𝑔(𝑎mod𝑐,𝑏mod𝑐,𝑐,𝑛)+⌊𝑎𝑐⌋2𝑛(𝑛+1)(2𝑛+1)6+⌊𝑏𝑐⌋2(𝑛+1)+⌊𝑎𝑐⌋⌊𝑏𝑐⌋𝑛(𝑛+1).g(a,b,c,n)=g(amodc,bmodc,c,n)+⌊ac⌋n(n+1)(2n+1)6+⌊bc⌋n(n+1)2,h(a,b,c,n)=h(amodc,bmodc,c,n)+2⌊bc⌋f(amodc,bmodc,c,n)+2⌊ac⌋g(amodc,bmodc,c,n)+⌊ac⌋2n(n+1)(2n+1)6+⌊bc⌋2(n+1)+⌊ac⌋⌊bc⌋n(n+1).

    Then, by swapping the order of summation, we can further transform. Similarly, let:

    𝑚=⌊𝑎𝑛+𝑏𝑐⌋.m=⌊an+bc⌋.

    Then for the sum 𝑔g:

    𝑔(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑖=0𝑖⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋=𝑛∑𝑖=0𝑚−1∑𝑗=0𝑖[𝑗<⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋]=𝑚−1∑𝑗=0𝑛∑𝑖=0𝑖[𝑖>⌊𝑐𝑗+𝑐−𝑏−1𝑎⌋]=𝑚−1∑𝑗=012(⌊𝑐𝑗+𝑐−𝑏−1𝑎⌋+𝑛+1)(𝑛−⌊𝑐𝑗+𝑐−𝑏−1𝑎⌋)=12𝑚𝑛(𝑛+1)−12𝑚−1∑𝑗=0⌊𝑐𝑗+𝑐−𝑏−1𝑎⌋−12𝑚−1∑𝑗=0⌊𝑐𝑗+𝑐−𝑏−1𝑎⌋2=12𝑚𝑛(𝑛+1)−12𝑓(𝑐,𝑐−𝑏−1,𝑎,𝑚−1)−12ℎ(𝑐,𝑐−𝑏−1,𝑎,𝑚−1).g(a,b,c,n)=∑i=0ni⌊ai+bc⌋=∑i=0n∑j=0m−1i[j<⌊ai+bc⌋]=∑j=0m−1∑i=0ni[i>⌊cj+c−b−1a⌋]=∑j=0m−112(⌊cj+c−b−1a⌋+n+1)(n−⌊cj+c−b−1a⌋)=12mn(n+1)−12∑j=0m−1⌊cj+c−b−1a⌋−12∑j=0m−1⌊cj+c−b−1a⌋2=12mn(n+1)−12f(c,c−b−1,a,m−1)−12h(c,c−b−1,a,m−1).

    For the sum ℎh:

    ℎ(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑖=0⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋2=𝑛∑𝑖=0𝑚−1∑𝑗=0(2𝑗+1)[𝑗<⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋]=𝑚−1∑𝑗=0𝑛∑𝑖=0(2𝑗+1)[𝑖>⌊𝑐𝑗+𝑐−𝑏−1𝑎⌋]=𝑚−1∑𝑗=0(2𝑗+1)(𝑛−⌊𝑐𝑗+𝑐−𝑏−1𝑎⌋)=𝑛𝑚2−𝑚−1∑𝑗=0⌊𝑐𝑗+𝑐−𝑏−1𝑎⌋−2𝑚−1∑𝑗=0𝑗⌊𝑐𝑗+𝑐−𝑏−1𝑎⌋=𝑛𝑚2−𝑓(𝑐,𝑐−𝑏−1,𝑎,𝑚−1)−2𝑔(𝑐,𝑐−𝑏−1,𝑎,𝑚−1).h(a,b,c,n)=∑i=0n⌊ai+bc⌋2=∑i=0n∑j=0m−1(2j+1)[j<⌊ai+bc⌋]=∑j=0m−1∑i=0n(2j+1)[i>⌊cj+c−b−1a⌋]=∑j=0m−1(2j+1)(n−⌊cj+c−b−1a⌋)=nm2−∑j=0m−1⌊cj+c−b−1a⌋−2∑j=0m−1j⌊cj+c−b−1a⌋=nm2−f(c,c−b−1,a,m−1)−2g(c,c−b−1,a,m−1).

    From the geometric perspective, these nonlinear sums assign corresponding weights 𝑤(𝑖,𝑗)w(i,j) to each point (𝑖,𝑗)(i,j) in the region. Apart from these weights, the rest of the computation process is exactly the same. For the choice of weights, in general:

    𝑛∑𝑖=0𝑖𝑟⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋𝑠=𝑛∑𝑖=0𝑚−1∑𝑗=0𝑖𝑟((𝑗+1)𝑠−𝑗𝑠)[𝑗<⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋].∑i=0nir⌊ai+bc⌋s=∑i=0n∑j=0m−1ir((j+1)s−js)[j<⌊ai+bc⌋].

    Another characteristic of this problem is that 𝑔g and ℎh intersect each other during recursive computation. Therefore, (𝑓,𝑔,ℎ)(f,g,h) needs to be recursively computed as a triple.

    #include <iostream>

struct Data {
  int f, g, h;
};

Data solve(long long a, long long b, long long c, long long n) {
  constexpr long long M = 998244353;
  constexpr long long i2 = (M + 1) / 2;
  constexpr long long i6 = (M + 1) / 6;
  long long n2 = (n + 1) * n % M * i2 % M;
  long long n3 = (2 * n + 1) * (n + 1) % M * n % M * i6 % M;
  Data res = {0, 0, 0};
  if (a >= c || b >= c) {
    auto tmp = solve(a % c, b % c, c, n);
    long long aa = a / c, bb = b / c;
    res.f = (tmp.f + aa * n2 + bb * (n + 1)) % M;
    res.g = (tmp.g + aa * n3 + bb * n2) % M;
    res.h = (tmp.h + 2 * bb * tmp.f % M + 2 * aa * tmp.g % M +
             aa * aa % M * n3 % M + bb * bb % M * (n + 1) % M +
             2 * aa * bb % M * n2 % M) %
            M;
    return res;
  }
  long long m = (a * n + b) / c;
  if (!m) return res;
  auto tmp = solve(c, c - b - 1, a, m - 1);
  res.f = (m * n - tmp.f + M) % M;
  res.g = (m * n2 + (M - tmp.f) * i2 + (M - tmp.h) * i2) % M;
  res.h = (n * m % M * m - tmp.f - tmp.g * 2 + 3 * M) % M;
  return res;
}

int main() {
  int t;
  std::cin >> t;
  for (; t; --t) {
    int n, a, b, c;
    std::cin >> n >> a >> b >> c;
    auto res = solve(a, b, c, n);
    std::cout << res.f << ' ' << res.h << ' ' << res.g << '\n';
  }
  return 0;
}
    [Tsinghua Training 2014] Sum](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P5172)

    Multiple queries. Given positive integers 𝑛n and 𝑟r, find:

    𝑛∑𝑑=1(−1)⌊𝑑√𝑟⌋.∑d=1n(−1)⌊dr⌋.
    Solution One

    If 𝑟r is a perfect square, then when √𝑟r is even, the sum is 𝑛n; otherwise, the sum alternates between 00 and −1−1 depending on the parity of 𝑛n. Below we consider the case where 𝑟r is not a perfect square.

    To apply the Euclidean-like algorithm, first transform the summation into the familiar form:

    𝑛∑𝑑=1(−1)⌊𝑑√𝑟⌋=𝑛∑𝑑=1(1−2(⌊𝑑√𝑟⌋mod2))=𝑛−2𝑛∑𝑑=1(⌊𝑑√𝑟⌋−2⌊⌊𝑑√𝑟⌋2⌋)=𝑛−2𝑛∑𝑑=1⌊𝑑√𝑟⌋+4𝑛∑𝑑=1⌊𝑑√𝑟2⌋=𝑛−2𝑓(𝑛,1,0,1)+4𝑓(𝑛,1,0,2)∑d=1n(−1)⌊dr⌋=∑d=1n(1−2(⌊dr⌋mod2))=n−2∑d=1n(⌊dr⌋−2⌊⌊dr⌋2⌋)=n−2∑d=1n⌊dr⌋+4∑d=1n⌊dr2⌋=n−2f(n,1,0,1)+4f(n,1,0,2)

    The function 𝑓f here has the form:

    𝑓(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑖=1⌊𝑎√𝑟+𝑏𝑐𝑖⌋.f(a,b,c,n)=∑i=1n⌊ar+bci⌋.

    Different from the algorithm in the main text, the slope here is no longer a rational number. Let the slope be:

    𝑘=𝑎√𝑟+𝑏𝑐.k=ar+bc.

    Again, discuss in two cases. If 𝑘 ≥1k≥1, then:

    𝑓(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑖=1⌊𝑘𝑖⌋=𝑛∑𝑖=1⌊(𝑘−⌊𝑘⌋)𝑖⌋+⌊𝑘⌋𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑖=⌊𝑘⌋𝑛(𝑛+1)2+𝑓(𝑎,𝑏−𝑐⌊𝑘⌋,𝑐,𝑛).f(a,b,c,n)=∑i=1n⌊ki⌋=∑i=1n⌊(k−⌊k⌋)i⌋+⌊k⌋∑i=1ni=⌊k⌋n(n+1)2+f(a,b−c⌊k⌋,c,n).

    The problem transforms to the case where the slope is less than one. If 𝑘 <1k<1, let 𝑚 =⌊𝑛𝑘⌋m=⌊nk⌋:

    𝑓(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑖=1⌊𝑘𝑖⌋=𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑚∑𝑗=1[𝑗≤⌊𝑘𝑖⌋]=𝑚∑𝑗=1𝑛∑𝑖=1[𝑖>⌊𝑘−1𝑗⌋]=𝑛𝑚−𝑚∑𝑗=1𝑛∑𝑖=1[𝑖≤⌊𝑘−1𝑗⌋].f(a,b,c,n)=∑i=1n⌊ki⌋=∑i=1n∑j=1m[j≤⌊ki⌋]=∑j=1m∑i=1n[i>⌊k−1j⌋]=nm−∑j=1m∑i=1n[i≤⌊k−1j⌋].

    In this derivation, the condition for swapping 𝑖i and 𝑗j is simpler than in the main text because there are no lattice points on the line 𝑦 =𝑘𝑥y=kx except the origin. The key is to write the summed expression after swapping in the form 𝑓(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)f(a,b,c,n), which requires finding 𝑎′,𝑏′,𝑐′a′,b′,c′ satisfying:

    𝑘−1=𝑎′√𝑟+𝑏′𝑐′.k−1=a′r+b′c′.

    This is not difficult. By rationalizing the denominator:

    𝑘−1=𝑐𝑎√𝑟+𝑏=𝑐𝑎√𝑟−𝑐𝑏𝑎2𝑟−𝑏2.k−1=car+b=car−cba2r−b2.

    Therefore:

    𝑎′=𝑐𝑎, 𝑏′=−𝑐𝑏, 𝑐′=𝑎2𝑟−𝑏2.a′=ca, b′=−cb, c′=a2r−b2.

    This shows:

    𝑓(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑛𝑚−𝑓(𝑐𝑎,−𝑐𝑏,𝑎2𝑟−𝑏2,𝑚).f(a,b,c,n)=nm−f(ca,−cb,a2r−b2,m).

    To avoid integer overflow, we need to divide 𝑎,𝑏,𝑐a,b,c by their greatest common divisor each time. Since this computation process is exactly the same as the process of computing the continued fraction of 𝑘k, according to the continued fraction theory, as long as gcd(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐) =1gcd(a,b,c)=1, they are necessarily within the integer range during computation. Also, although (𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)(a,b,c,n) will not overflow, in the data range of this problem, 𝑓(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)f(a,b,c,n) may exceed the range of 64-bit integers, and natural overflow is fine; no special handling is needed, and the final result is definitely between [ −𝑛,𝑛][−n,n].

    Although the slope does not become zero, the complexity is still 𝑂(log⁡𝑛)O(log⁡n), which is easy to see from the previous proof of algorithm complexity.

    #include <cmath>
#include <iostream>

long long r;
long double sqrt_r;

long long gcd(long long a, long long b) { return b ? gcd(b, a % b) : a; }

unsigned long long f(long long a, long long b, long long c, long long n) {
  if (!n) return 0;
  auto d = gcd(a, gcd(b, c));
  a /= d;
  b /= d;
  c /= d;
  unsigned long long k = (a * sqrt_r + b) / c;
  if (k) {
    return n * (n + 1) / 2 * k + f(a, b - c * k, c, n);
  } else {
    unsigned long long m = n * (a * sqrt_r + b) / c;
    return n * m - f(c * a, -c * b, a * a * r - b * b, m);
  }
}

unsigned long long solve(long long n, long long r) {
  long long sqr = sqrt_r = sqrtl(r);
  if (r == sqr * sqr) return r % 2 ? (n % 2 ? -1 : 0) : n;
  return n - 2 * f(1, 0, 1, n) + 4 * f(1, 0, 2, n);
}

int main() {
  int t;
  std::cin >> t;
  for (; t; --t) {
    int n;
    std::cin >> n >> r;
    long long res = solve(n, r);
    std::cout << res << '\n';
  }
  return 0;
}
    Fraction

    Given positive integers 𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑑a,b,c,d, find the reduced fraction 𝑝/𝑞p/q that satisfies 𝑎/𝑏 <𝑝/𝑞 <𝑐/𝑑a/b<p/q<c/d and has the smallest lexicographic order (𝑞,𝑝)(q,p).

    Solution

    This problem is also a classic application of the Stern-Brocot tree. The solution can be found at there. Since it only depends on the recursive structure of fractions, it can also be solved using the Euclidean-like algorithm method, so it can also be regarded as an application of the Euclidean-like algorithm.

    If there is at least one natural number between 𝑎/𝑏a/b and 𝑐/𝑑c/d (not including endpoints), we can directly take (𝑞,𝑝) =(1,⌊𝑎/𝑏⌋ +1)(q,p)=(1,⌊a/b⌋+1). Otherwise, we necessarily have:

    ⌊𝑎𝑏⌋≤𝑎𝑏<𝑝𝑞<𝑐𝑑≤⌊𝑎𝑏⌋+1.⌊ab⌋≤ab<pq<cd≤⌊ab⌋+1.

    From this inequality, the integer part of 𝑝/𝑞p/q can be determined as ⌊𝑎/𝑏⌋⌊a/b⌋. Then eliminate this integer part and take the reciprocal to determine its fractional part. This is exactly the basic method for determining the continued fraction of 𝑝/𝑞p/q. If the final answer is 𝑝/𝑞p/q, the time complexity of the algorithm is 𝑂(log⁡min{𝑝,𝑞})O(log⁡min{p,q}).

    Here, there is a detail problem: whether the fraction with the smallest lexicographic order after taking the reciprocal is the same as before taking the reciprocal. In other words, among fractions 𝑝/𝑞p/q satisfying 𝑎/𝑏 <𝑝/𝑞 <𝑐/𝑑a/b<p/q<c/d, is the one with the smallest lexicographic order (𝑞,𝑝)(q,p) also the one with the smallest lexicographic order (𝑝,𝑞)(p,q)? Suppose not. Let 𝑝/𝑞p/q be the one with the smallest lexicographic order (𝑞,𝑝)(q,p), but 𝑟/𝑠 ≠𝑝/𝑞r/s≠p/q is the one with the smallest lexicographic order (𝑟,𝑠)(r,s). This necessarily has 𝑟 <𝑝r<p and 𝑞 <𝑠q<s. But this shows:

    𝑎𝑏<𝑟𝑠<𝑟𝑞<𝑝𝑞<𝑐𝑑.ab<rs<rq<pq<cd.

    Therefore, 𝑟/𝑞r/q is strictly smaller than the current solution in whichever lexicographic order. This contradicts the assumption. Therefore, the above algorithm is correct.

    #include <iostream>

void solve(int a, int b, int& p, int& q, int c, int d) {
  if ((a / b + 1) * d < c) {
    p = a / b + 1;
    q = 1;
  } else {
    solve(d, c - d * (a / b), q, p, b, a % b);
    p += q * (a / b);
  }
}

int main() {
  int a, b, c, d, p, q;
  while (std::cin >> a >> b >> c >> d) {
    solve(a, b, p, q, c, d);
    std::cout << p << '/' << q << '\n';
  }
  return 0;
}

    Universal Euclidean Algorithm

    The derivation of the Euclidean-like algorithm discussed in the previous section is usually relatively cumbersome, and the summations it can solve are mainly summations that can be transformed into counting (weighted) integer points under a line. This section discusses a more general method that further abstracts the above process, so it can solve more problems. Therefore, this method is also called the Universal Euclidean Algorithm. It also uses the recursive structure of fractions to solve problems, but the way it reduces the problem is slightly different from the Euclidean-like algorithm.

    Still consider the classic summation:

    𝑓(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑖=1⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋,f(a,b,c,n)=∑i=1n⌊ai+bc⌋,

    where 𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛a,b,c,n are all positive integers.

    Problem Transformation

    Define the segment with parameters (𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)(a,b,c,n) as:

    𝑦=𝑎𝑥+𝑏𝑐, 0<𝑥≤𝑛.y=ax+bc, 0<x≤n.

    For this segment, we can define a string composed of 𝑈U and 𝑅R as follows, also called the operation sequence:

    • The string consists of exactly 𝑛n 𝑅R's and 𝑚 =⌊(𝑎𝑛 +𝑏)/𝑐⌋m=⌊(an+b)/c⌋ 𝑈U's;
    • The number of 𝑈U's before the 𝑖i-th 𝑅R is exactly ⌊(𝑎𝑖 +𝑏)/𝑐⌋⌊(ai+b)/c⌋, where 𝑖 =1,⋯,𝑛i=1,⋯,n.

    From the geometric perspective, this is roughly equivalent to starting from the origin, writing an 𝑅R each time we cross a vertical grid line to the right, and writing a 𝑈U each time we cross a horizontal grid line upward. As shown in the figure:

    Of course, such a definition also needs to consider several special cases:

    • When passing through a lattice point (i.e., crossing up and right simultaneously), first write 𝑈U then 𝑅R:
    • At the beginning of the string, in addition to the number of times crossing the grid line upward in the interval (0,1](0,1], we need to additionally add ⌊𝑏/𝑐⌋⌊b/c⌋ 𝑈U's;
    • At the end of the string, there should be no extra 𝑈U's.

    If the description of the geometric perspective is unclear, you can refer to the definition in the algebraic method above to assist understanding. The description of geometric perspective helps understand the algorithm process below.

    The basic idea of the Universal Euclidean Algorithm is to treat both 𝑈U and 𝑅R in the operation sequence as elements of some monoid, and treat the entire operation sequence as the product of elements in the monoid, with the final answer related to this product.

    For example, in this problem, we can define the state vector 𝑣 =(1,𝑦,∑𝑦)v=(1,y,∑y), which represents the current state after starting from the origin and crossing several grid lines upward and rightward. Here, the first component is a constant, the second component is the 𝑦y-coordinate, and the third component is the required sum. Initially, we have 𝑣 =(1,0,0)v=(1,0,0). Each time we cross upward across a grid line, the 𝑦y-coordinate increases by one, which is equivalent to multiplying the state vector on the right by the matrix:

    𝑈=⎛⎜ ⎜ ⎜⎝110010001⎞⎟ ⎟ ⎟⎠.U=(110010001).

    Each time we cross right across a grid line, the sum increases by the 𝑦y-coordinate, which is equivalent to multiplying the state vector on the right by the matrix:

    𝑅=⎛⎜ ⎜ ⎜⎝100011001⎞⎟ ⎟ ⎟⎠.R=(100011001).

    Therefore, the final state is the product (1,0,0)𝑆(1,0,0)S, where 𝑆S is understood as the product of the above matrices. The answer we want is the third component of the final state.

    In addition to defining elements in the monoid as matrices, we can also define the contribution of a segment of operation sequence to the final result, and then define the product of operations as the combination of the contributions of two segments of operation sequences.

    In this problem, we can define the contribution of each segment of operation sequence as (𝑥,𝑦,∑𝑦)(x,y,∑y). To rigorously explain these notations, we can consider these components as functions of the operation sequence. That is, for an operation sequence 𝑆S, its contribution can be written as (𝑥(𝑆),𝑦(𝑆),(∑𝑦)(𝑆))(x(S),y(S),(∑y)(S)). Here, 𝑥(𝑆)x(S) and 𝑦(𝑆)y(S) respectively correspond to the number of 𝑅R's and 𝑈U's in the operation sequence 𝑆S, which is the number of times this segment crosses rightward and upward across grid lines. For the function 𝑓f on an operation sequence, we can define (∑𝑓)(𝑆)(∑f)(S), or write as ∑𝑆𝑓∑Sf, as the following expression:

    ∑𝑆𝑓:=∑{𝑓(𝑆[1,𝑟]):𝑆𝑟=𝑅}.∑Sf:=∑{f(S[1,r]):Sr=R}.

    Here, 𝑆𝑟Sr is the 𝑟r-th character in 𝑆S, and 𝑆[1,𝑟]S[1,r] is the prefix of the first 𝑟r characters in 𝑆S. That is, this summation notation can be seen as the summation over all prefixes of 𝑆S ending with 𝑅R. For example:

    ∑𝑆1=𝑥, ∑𝑆𝑥=12𝑥(𝑥+1).∑S1=x, ∑Sx=12x(x+1).

    For another example, ∑𝑦∑y is the accumulated number of times crossing upward across grid lines each time crossing rightward across a grid line. For the entire operation sequence, the values of 𝑦y at all prefixes ending with 𝑅R are exactly all the values ⌊(𝑎𝑖 +𝑏)/𝑐⌋⌊(ai+b)/c⌋ at 𝑖 =1,⋯,𝑛i=1,⋯,n. Therefore, computing ∑𝑦∑y for the entire operation sequence is exactly the quantity required in this problem.

    Initially, we have 𝑈 =(0,1,0)U=(0,1,0), 𝑅 =(1,0,0)R=(1,0,0). Moreover, we can define the product of two elements (𝑥1,𝑦1,𝑠1)(x1,y1,s1) and (𝑥2,𝑦2,𝑠2)(x2,y2,s2) as:

    (𝑥1,𝑦1,𝑠1)⋅(𝑥2,𝑦2,𝑠2)=(𝑥1+𝑥2,𝑦1+𝑦2,𝑠1+𝑠2+𝑥2𝑦1).(x1,y1,s1)⋅(x2,y2,s2)=(x1+x2,y1+y2,s1+s2+x2y1).

    Here, the last term in the contribution of the combined result can be obtained by the following calculation:

    ∑𝑆1+𝑆2𝑦=∑𝑆1𝑦+∑𝑆2(𝑦+𝑦1)=∑𝑆1𝑦+∑𝑆2𝑦+𝑦1∑𝑆21=𝑠1+𝑠2+𝑥2𝑦1.∑S1+S2y=∑S1y+∑S2(y+y1)=∑S1y+∑S2y+y1∑S21=s1+s2+x2y1.

    It is easy to verify that this multiplication operation satisfies the associativity law, and the identity element is (0,0,0)(0,0,0), so these elements form a monoid under this multiplication operation. The answer we want is the third component of the product.

    Both methods can get the correct results. However, because the matrix operation retains more redundant information and has a larger constant, the second method is more practical when dealing with actual problems.

    Algorithm Process

    Different from the overall reduction of the Euclidean-like algorithm, the Universal Euclidean Algorithm reduces the problem by combining these operations in batches. Let the product of operations corresponding to the string be:

    𝐹(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛,𝑈,𝑅).F(a,b,c,n,U,R).

    The reduction process is as follows:

    • When 𝑏 ≥𝑐b≥c, at the beginning of the operation sequence, there are ⌊𝑏/𝑐⌋⌊b/c⌋ 𝑈U's. Directly compute their product, and remove these 𝑈U's from the operation sequence. At this time, the number of 𝑈U's before the 𝑖i-th 𝑅R is:

      ⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋−⌊𝑏𝑐⌋=⌊𝑎𝑖+(𝑏mod𝑐)𝑐⌋.⌊ai+bc⌋−⌊bc⌋=⌊ai+(bmodc)c⌋.

      This is equivalent to changing the segment parameters from (𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)(a,b,c,n) to (𝑎,𝑏mod𝑐,𝑐,𝑛)(a,bmodc,c,n). So for this case:

      𝐹(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛,𝑈,𝑅)=𝑈⌊𝑏/𝑐⌋𝐹(𝑎,𝑏mod𝑐,𝑐,𝑛,𝑈,𝑅).F(a,b,c,n,U,R)=U⌊b/c⌋F(a,bmodc,c,n,U,R).

    • When 𝑎 ≥𝑐a≥c, in the operation sequence, each 𝑅R has at least ⌊𝑎/𝑐⌋⌊a/c⌋ 𝑈U's in front of it, which can be combined into 𝑅R. That is, 𝑅R can be replaced by 𝑈⌊𝑎/𝑐⌋𝑅U⌊a/c⌋R. In the combined string, the number of 𝑈U's before the 𝑖i-th 𝑅R is:

      ⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋−⌊𝑎𝑐⌋𝑖=⌊(𝑎mod𝑐)𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋.⌊ai+bc⌋−⌊ac⌋i=⌊(amodc)i+bc⌋.

      This is equivalent to changing the segment parameters from (𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)(a,b,c,n) to (𝑎mod𝑐,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛)(amodc,b,c,n). So for this case:

      𝐹(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛,𝑈,𝑅)=𝐹(𝑎mod𝑐,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛,𝑈,𝑈⌊𝑎/𝑐⌋𝑅).F(a,b,c,n,U,R)=F(amodc,b,c,n,U,U⌊a/c⌋R).

    • For the remaining cases, we need to flip the 𝑥x and 𝑦y axes, which basically swaps 𝑈U and 𝑅R, but the segment parameters after flipping need to be carefully calculated. Combined with the definition of the operation sequence, we need to determine coefficients (𝑎′,𝑏′,𝑐′,𝑛′)(a′,b′,c′,n′) such that in the operation sequence before flipping, the number of 𝑅R's before the 𝑗j-th 𝑈U is exactly ⌊(𝑎′𝑗 +𝑏′)/𝑐′⌋⌊(a′j+b′)/c′⌋ and there are a total of 𝑛′n′ 𝑈U's. According to the definition:

      𝑛′=⌊𝑎𝑛+𝑏𝑐⌋=𝑚,n′=⌊an+bc⌋=m,

      And the number of 𝑅R's before the 𝑗j-th 𝑈U is the largest 𝑖i such that:

      ⌊𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐⌋<𝑗⟺𝑎𝑖+𝑏𝑐<𝑗⟺𝑖<𝑐𝑗−𝑏𝑎⟺𝑖<⌈𝑐𝑗−𝑏𝑎⌉=⌊𝑐𝑗−𝑏−1𝑎⌋+1.⌊ai+bc⌋<j⟺ai+bc<j⟺i<cj−ba⟺i<⌈cj−ba⌉=⌊cj−b−1a⌋+1.

      Therefore, 𝑖 =⌊(𝑐𝑗 −𝑏 −1)/𝑎⌋i=⌊(cj−b−1)/a⌋. This derivation process is similar to the derivation of the Euclidean-like algorithm above, and also uses the properties of floor and ceiling functions.

      There are two details to handle:

      • The intercept term −(𝑏 +1)/𝑎−(b+1)/a is negative. Note that if we shift the segment left by one unit, the intercept term becomes positive because (𝑐 −𝑏 −1)/𝑎 ≥0(c−b−1)/a≥0. Therefore, we can extract the first 𝑅⌊(𝑐−𝑏−1)/𝑎⌋𝑈R⌊(c−b−1)/a⌋U and only swap 𝑈U and 𝑅R in the remaining operation sequence;
      • After swapping 𝑈U and 𝑅R, there are extra 𝑈U's at the end. Therefore, before swapping 𝑈U and 𝑅R, we need to first extract the last 𝑅R, and only swap 𝑈U and 𝑅R in the remaining operation sequence. The number of this segment of 𝑅R is 𝑛 −⌊(𝑐𝑚 −𝑏 −1)/𝑎⌋n−⌊(cm−b−1)/a⌋.

      After removing several characters at the beginning and end, the number of 𝑅R's before the 𝑗j-th 𝑈U becomes:

      ⌊𝑐(𝑗+1)−𝑏−1𝑎⌋−⌊𝑐−𝑏−1𝑎⌋=⌊𝑐𝑗+(𝑐−𝑏−1)mod𝑎𝑎⌋.⌊c(j+1)−b−1a⌋−⌊c−b−1a⌋=⌊cj+(c−b−1)modaa⌋.

      Recall that the number of 𝑈U's before flipping is 𝑚 =⌊(𝑎𝑛 +𝑏)/𝑐⌋m=⌊(an+b)/c⌋. And this shift by one unit requires that there is at least one 𝑈U before flipping, i.e., 𝑚 >0m>0. Using this condition, we can divide into two cases:

      • For the case 𝑚 >0m>0, after handling the above two points, the operation sequence after swapping 𝑈U and 𝑅R is exactly the valid sequence corresponding to the segment with parameters (𝑐,(𝑐 −𝑏 −1)mod𝑎,𝑎,𝑚 −1)(c,(c−b−1)moda,a,m−1). Therefore:

        𝐹(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛,𝑈,𝑅)=𝑅⌊(𝑐−𝑏−1)/𝑎⌋𝑈𝐹(𝑐,(𝑐−𝑏−1)mod𝑎,𝑎,𝑚−1,𝑅,𝑈)𝑅𝑛−⌊(𝑐𝑚−𝑏−1)/𝑎⌋.F(a,b,c,n,U,R)=R⌊(c−b−1)/a⌋UF(c,(c−b−1)moda,a,m−1,R,U)Rn−⌊(cm−b−1)/a⌋.

      • Especially for the case 𝑚 =0m=0, the operation sequence before swapping only contains 𝑛n 𝑅R's, and we can return directly:

        𝐹(𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑛,𝑈,𝑅)=𝑅𝑛.F(a,b,c,n,U,R)=Rn.

        Different from the Euclidean-like algorithm, this special case of the Universal Euclidean Algorithm needs to be handled separately, otherwise it cannot be calculated correctly due to involving negative exponents.

    Using these discussions, the problem can be solved recursively.

    Assume that the time complexity of a single multiplication of elements in the monoid is 𝑂(1)O(1). Then, if all exponent calculations of these elements during the computation use fast exponentiation, the final algorithm complexity is 𝑂(log⁡max{𝑎,𝑐} +log⁡(𝑏/𝑐))O(log⁡max{a,c}+log⁡(b/c))1.

    Explanation of Complexity

    Comparing with the (Euclidean) Euclidean algorithm, the Universal Euclidean Algorithm just adds the step of fast exponentiation. The rest of the computation process has a complexity similar to the Euclidean-like algorithm, which has been shown to be 𝑂(log⁡min{𝑎,𝑐,𝑛})O(log⁡min{a,c,n}). Now we need to compute the total complexity of these fast exponentiations.

    Except for the first iteration, we have 𝑏 <𝑐b<c, so each of these iterations involves three fast exponentiation calculations, with a total complexity of:

    𝑂(log⁡⌊𝑎𝑐⌋+log⁡⌊𝑐−𝑏1−1𝑎1⌋+log⁡(𝑛−⌊𝑐𝑚−𝑏1−1𝑎1⌋)),O(log⁡⌊ac⌋+log⁡⌊c−b1−1a1⌋+log⁡(n−⌊cm−b1−1a1⌋)),

    where 𝑎1 =𝑎mod𝑐a1=amodc, 𝑏1 =𝑏mod𝑐b1=bmodc and 𝑚 =⌊(𝑎1𝑛 +𝑏1)/𝑐⌋m=⌊(a1n+b1)/c⌋. For the latter two, we have estimates:

    𝑐−𝑏1−1𝑎1≤𝑐𝑎1,𝑛−⌊𝑐𝑚−𝑏1−1𝑎1⌋≤𝑛−𝑐𝑚−𝑏1−1𝑎1+1≤𝑛−𝑐((𝑎1𝑛+𝑏1)/𝑐−1)−𝑏1−1𝑎1+1=𝑐+1𝑎1+1.c−b1−1a1≤ca1,n−⌊cm−b1−1a1⌋≤n−cm−b1−1a1+1≤n−c((a1n+b1)/c−1)−b1−1a1+1=c+1a1+1.

    Therefore, the complexity of these two is 𝑂(log⁡(𝑐/𝑎1))O(log⁡(c/a1)).

    In each iteration, the segment parameters change from (𝑎, ⋅,𝑐, ⋅)(a,⋅,c,⋅) to (𝑐, ⋅,𝑎mod𝑐, ⋅)(c,⋅,amodc,⋅), and the total time complexity of the round is:

    𝑂(log⁡𝑎𝑐+log⁡𝑐𝑎mod𝑐).O(log⁡ac+log⁡camodc).

    For all rounds of recursion, these terms can be canceled by splitting, so the total complexity is 𝑂(log⁡𝑎 +log⁡𝑐) =𝑂(log⁡max{𝑎,𝑐})O(log⁡a+log⁡c)=O(log⁡max{a,c}).

    Finally, plus the complexity of the first iteration of fast exponentiation 𝑈⌊𝑏/𝑐⌋U⌊b/c⌋, which is 𝑂(log⁡(𝑏/𝑐))O(log⁡(b/c)), we get the total complexity 𝑂(log⁡max{𝑎,𝑐} +log⁡(𝑏/𝑐))O(log⁡max{a,c}+log⁡(b/c)).

    The process of the Universal Euclidean Algorithm can be written as a unified template. When dealing with specific problems, we only need to change the implementation of the template type T.

    // Class T implements the monoid.
// Assume that it provides a multiplication operator
//     and a default constructor returning the unity in the monoid.

// Binary exponentiation.
template <typename T>
T pow(T a, int b) {
  T res;
  for (; b; b >>= 1) {
    if (b & 1) res = res * a;
    a = a * a;
  }
  return res;
}

// Universal Euclidean algorithm.
template <typename T>
T euclid(int a, int b, int c, int n, T U, T R) {
  if (b >= c) return pow(U, b / c) * euclid(a, b % c, c, n, U, R);
  if (a >= c) return euclid(a % c, b, c, n, U, pow(U, a / c) * R);
  auto m = ((long long)a * n + b) / c;
  if (!m) return pow(R, n);
  return pow(R, (c - b - 1) / a) * U *
         euclid(c, (c - b - 1) % a, a, m - 1, R, U) *
         pow(R, n - (c * m - b - 1) / a);
}

    #include <array>
#include <iostream>

// Switch between matrix and info merging approaches.
#define MATRIX 1

// Class T implements the monoid.
// Assume that it provides a multiplication operator
//     and a default constructor returning the unity in the monoid.

// Binary exponentiation.
template <typename T>
T pow(T a, int b) {
  T res;
  for (; b; b >>= 1) {
    if (b & 1) res = res * a;
    a = a * a;
  }
  return res;
}

// Universal Euclidean algorithm.
template <typename T>
T euclid(int a, int b, int c, int n, T U, T R) {
  if (b >= c) return pow(U, b / c) * euclid(a, b % c, c, n, U, R);
  if (a >= c) return euclid(a % c, b, c, n, U, pow(U, a / c) * R);
  auto m = ((long long)a * n + b) / c;
  if (!m) return pow(R, n);
  return pow(R, (c - b - 1) / a) * U *
         euclid(c, (c - b - 1) % a, a, m - 1, R, U) *
         pow(R, n - (c * m - b - 1) / a);
}

#if MATRIX

template <size_t N>
struct Matrix {
  std::array<long long, N * N> mat;

  auto loc(size_t i, size_t j) const { return mat[i * N + j]; }

  auto& loc(size_t i, size_t j) { return mat[i * N + j]; }

  Matrix() : mat{} {
    for (size_t i = 0; i != N; ++i) {
      loc(i, i) = 1;
    }
  }

  Matrix operator*(const Matrix& rhs) const {
    Matrix res;
    res.mat.fill(0);
    for (size_t i = 0; i != N; ++i) {
      for (size_t k = 0; k != N; ++k) {
        for (size_t j = 0; j != N; ++j) {
          res.loc(i, j) += loc(i, k) * rhs.loc(k, j);
        }
      }
    }
    return res;
  }
};

long long solve(int a, int b, int c, int n) {
  if (!n) return 0;
  Matrix<3> U, R;
  U.loc(0, 1) = R.loc(1, 2) = 1;
  auto res = euclid(a, b, c, n, U, R);
  return res.loc(0, 2);
}

#else

struct Info {
  long long x, y, s;

  Info() : x(0), y(0), s(0) {}

  Info operator*(const Info& rhs) const {
    Info res;
    res.x = x + rhs.x;
    res.y = y + rhs.y;
    res.s = s + rhs.s + rhs.x * y;
    return res;
  }
};

long long solve(int a, int b, int c, int n) {
  if (!n) return 0;
  Info U, R;
  U.y = 1;
  R.x = 1;
  auto res = euclid(a, b, c, n, U, R);
  return res.s;
}

#endif

int main() {
  int t;
  std::cin >> t;
  for (; t; --t) {
    int a, b, c, n;
    std::cin >> n >> c >> a >> b;
    std::cout << solve(a, b, c, n - 1) << '\n';
  }
  return 0;
}

    #include <iostream>

template <typename T>
T pow(T a, int b) {
  T res;
  for (; b; b >>= 1) {
    if (b & 1) res = res * a;
    a = a * a;
  }
  return res;
}

template <typename T>
T euclid(int a, int b, int c, int n, T U, T R) {
  if (b >= c) return pow(U, b / c) * euclid(a, b % c, c, n, U, R);
  if (a >= c) return euclid(a % c, b, c, n, U, pow(U, a / c) * R);
  auto m = ((long long)a * n + b) / c;
  if (!m) return pow(R, n);
  return pow(R, (c - b - 1) / a) * U *
         euclid(c, (c - b - 1) % a, a, m - 1, R, U) *
         pow(R, n - (c * m - b - 1) / a);
}

constexpr int M = 998244353;

struct Info {
  long long x, y, s, t, u;

  Info() : x(0), y(0), s(0), t(0), u(0) {}

  Info operator*(const Info& rhs) const {
    Info res;
    res.x = (x + rhs.x) % M;
    res.y = (y + rhs.y) % M;
    res.s = (s + rhs.s + rhs.x * y) % M;
    auto tmp = (rhs.x * (rhs.x + 1) / 2 + x * rhs.x) % M;
    res.t = (t + rhs.t + x * rhs.s + tmp * y) % M;
    res.u = (u + rhs.u + 2 * y * rhs.s + rhs.x * y % M * y) % M;
    return res;
  }
};

void solve(int a, int b, int c, int n) {
  Info U, R;
  U.y = 1;
  R.x = 1;
  auto res = euclid(a, b, c, n, U, R);
  auto f = (res.s + b / c) % M;
  auto g = res.t;
  auto h = (res.u + (long long)(b / c) * (b / c)) % M;
  std::cout << f << ' ' << h << ' ' << g << '\n';
}

int main() {
  int t;
  std::cin >> t;
  for (; t; --t) {
    int a, b, c, n;
    std::cin >> n >> a >> b >> c;
    solve(a, b, c, n);
  }
  return 0;
}
    [Tsinghua Training 2014] Sum](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P5172)

    Multiple queries. Given positive integers 𝑛n and 𝑟r, find:

    𝑛∑𝑑=1(−1)⌊𝑑√𝑟⌋.∑d=1n(−1)⌊dr⌋.
    Solution Two

    First, handle the case where 𝑟r is a perfect square separately, which is completely consistent with the above and is omitted. Here, we only consider the case where 𝑟r is not a perfect square.

    There are many ways to apply the Universal Euclidean Algorithm to this problem. For example, we can define a linear transformation for each operation:

    𝑈(𝑥)=−𝑥, 𝑅(𝑥)=𝑥+1.U(x)=−x, R(x)=x+1.

    The multiplication of operations is defined as the composition of linear transformations. Then the final answer is the value at 𝑥 =0x=0 of the function obtained by composing the transformations corresponding to the operation sequence.

    We can also define the contribution of each segment of the operation sequence. The contribution can be defined as (( −1)𝑦,∑( −1)𝑦)((−1)y,∑(−1)y). Then the two operations are respectively:

    𝑈=(0,−1), 𝑅=(1,1).U=(0,−1), R=(1,1).

    The combination of contributions is defined as:

    (𝑢1,𝑣1)⋅(𝑢2,𝑣2)=(𝑢1𝑢2,𝑣1+𝑢1𝑣2).(u1,v1)⋅(u2,v2)=(u1u2,v1+u1v2).

    It is easy to verify that under this multiplication, all operations form a monoid, and the identity element is (0,1)(0,1). The final answer is the second component of the product of all elements.

    These two methods are consistent, because if the linear transformation is written as 𝑓(𝑥) =𝑢 +𝑣𝑥f(x)=u+vx, then the change of coefficients corresponding to the composition of linear transformations is exactly the multiplication of operations above. That is, these two monoids are isomorphic.

    In this problem, the segment parameters are (𝑘,𝑛)(k,n), where 𝑘 ∈𝐑k∈R is the slope of the line. Let the product of the operation sequence be 𝐹(𝑘,𝑛,𝑈,𝑅)F(k,n,U,R). Then we have the following recursive algorithm:

    • If 𝑘 ≥1k≥1, then in the operation sequence, each 𝑅R has at least ⌊𝑘⌋⌊k⌋ 𝑈U's in front of it. Therefore:

      𝐹(𝑘,𝑛,𝑈,𝑅)=𝐹(𝑘−⌊𝑘⌋,𝑛,𝑈,𝑈⌊𝑘⌋𝑅).F(k,n,U,R)=F(k−⌊k⌋,n,U,U⌊k⌋R).

    • If 𝑘 <1k<1, then swap 𝑈U and 𝑅R in the operation sequence and discard the trailing 𝑈U's (i.e., the 𝑅R's before swapping). Therefore:

      𝐹(𝑘,𝑛,𝑈,𝑅)=𝐹(𝑘−1,𝑚,𝑅,𝑈)𝑅𝑛−⌊𝑘−1𝑚⌋.F(k,n,U,R)=F(k−1,m,R,U)Rn−⌊k−1m⌋.

    In this algorithm, the iteration process of 𝑘k is actually the continued fraction expansion of √𝑟r. For this, we can apply the PQa Algorithm. The process of finding the continued fraction and the iteration process of the Universal Euclidean Algorithm can be done simultaneously.

    Consistent with the case of the Euclidean-like algorithm, the complexity of this algorithm is still 𝑂(log⁡𝑛)O(log⁡n).

    #include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>

template <typename T>
T pow(T a, int b) {
  T res;
  for (; b; b >>= 1) {
    if (b & 1) res = res * a;
    a = a * a;
  }
  return res;
}

struct LinearTransform {
  int u, v;

  LinearTransform() : u(0), v(1) {}

  LinearTransform operator*(const LinearTransform& rhs) const {
    LinearTransform res;
    res.u = u + v * rhs.u;
    res.v = v * rhs.v;
    return res;
  }

  int eval(int x) const { return u + v * x; }
};

int solve(int n, int r) {
  long double sqrt_r = sqrtl(r);
  int sqr = sqrt_r;
  if (r == sqr * sqr) return sqr % 2 ? (n % 2 ? -1 : 0) : n;
  int P = 0, Q = 1, D = r, val = 0;
  LinearTransform U, R;
  U.v = -1;
  R.u = 1;
  while (n) {
    int a = (P + sqr) / Q;
    R = pow(U, a) * R;
    int m = ((P + sqrt_r) / Q - a) * n;
    P = a * Q - P;
    Q = (D - P * P) / Q;
    int rem = n - (int)(m * (P + sqrt_r) / Q);
    val = pow(R, rem).eval(val);
    std::swap(U, R);
    n = m;
  }
  return val;
}

int main() {
  int t;
  std::cin >> t;
  for (; t; --t) {
    int n, r;
    std::cin >> n >> r;
    std::cout << solve(n, r) << '\n';
  }
  return 0;
}

    1. In problems usually considered, 𝑏b is of the same order as 𝑎a, and 𝑂(log⁡(𝑏/𝑐))O(log⁡(b/c)) can be ignored. Moreover, if before calling the Universal Euclidean Algorithm, we first perform a round of modulo reduction in the Euclidean-like algorithm to eliminate the impact of 𝑏b, the complexity of fast exponentiation of this term can be avoided. This is because in usual problems, the initial form of 𝑈U is relatively special, and its powers have simpler forms and do not need to be calculated by fast exponentiation. For example, in the main text, the result of 𝑈⌊𝑏/𝑎⌋U⌊b/a⌋ is obtained by replacing the 11 not on the diagonal in 𝑈U with ⌊𝑏/𝑎⌋⌊b/a⌋, without using fast exponentiation. ↩
